utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-08-91-T, the Prosecutor versus Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Good morning to everyone. May we take the appearances today, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry. Good morning, Your Honours. Joanna Korner and Crispian Smith for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. For the Stanisic Defence, Slobodan Cvijetic and Ms. Deirdre Montgomery.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Dragan Krgovic and Miroslav Cuskic, appearing for Zupljanin Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, before the General starts, I was given certain information by Mr. Krgovic about something that happened over the weekend. And Your Honours have been told, have you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: We've been enlightened, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's been raised, has it? Okay, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Can we go to the private session for this purpose, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, we go into private session.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm sorry to interrupt and I would thought it would have been better to discuss it in the absence of the General. I'm a little concerned - because I have a lot of questions for the General and in some detail - whether he feels fit enough. We won't -- we weren't told anything about this by VWS, nor do we know what the medical prognosis was. And obviously I don't want it to be thought at any stage that I'm taking an unfair advantage of the General ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Please continue, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, for the record, we're in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Oh. Can we go back into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. We rise, to resume at 9.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: --- Break taken at 9.13 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: The witness may be escorted back in. And we could go into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: General, last thing on Friday, you took with you the reports done by Mr. Brown, Dr. Nielsen, and Richard Butler, the last you'd read for your previous report. All I want to ask you about that is this: Do you agree that, having re-read Mr. Butler's report, it deals with the VRS in terms of what happened at Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, as far as I remember, Mr. Butler's report that I mentioned, first and foremost, deals with the command responsibility of the corps command.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. At the time, 1995, of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that Mr. Butler dealt with 1992, with the command, and the prerogatives of the command of the corps, as far as I remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I accept that he dealt with the overall, if you like, philosophy of command and control, within the VRS, and certainly at the period. But, largely, dealing with it in the light of the events at Srebrenica. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam, I dealt with 1992 in my report, not with 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, let's see if you will accept this. It's right - isn't it? - that he doesn't look at anything to do with the relationship between the VRS and the RS MUP.

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I remember correctly, Mr. Butler did not analyse these relationships.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The second matter I want to just ask you about in respect of your evidence last Friday is this: Is it right that you left Croatia and moved to Bihac in November of 1991?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Or, to be more precise, in late November. I think it was the 28th or the 29th of November. But it's been a long time.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. And have you personally ever commanded a -- a group of soldiers that included resubordinated police?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand your question, Ms. Korner. But I must say that the topic I dealt with, and that is the use of the police in combat activities and its resubordination, as well as the command relationship that comes into being then, does not require me to have done anything like it personally. That matter is regulated by military rules and regulations which I had the opportunity to get acquainted with during my military career. That matter seemed to be the principal problem, to me. And I wanted to assist you and the Trial Chamber by explaining this matter through the rules and regulations.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. I take it from that, that your answer to the actual question I asked, which is: Had you ever personally commanded a group of soldiers in combat, which included resubordinated police, is no?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. If you insist on getting an answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm afraid it is important because at a later stage your evidence is going to be read. And, therefore, as you say, your evidence about this is based on your study of military laws, regulations, and some documents?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now, can we please look, first of all, at some of the differences between the report you wrote for this case and the report you did for the Popovic case, on the same topics. This is no criticism, General. It's right, isn't it, you used the Popovic report, the report you wrote for General Gvero, as a starting point, if nothing else, for this present report?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is correct that I used parts of my earlier report. But since we're talking about two reports, I must point out the fact that they deal with two completely different topics.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, they don't, in fact, entirely, do they, because the bulk of your report in both cases was concerned with command and control issues as laid down in the regulations of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In order to explain the subject matter I researched, I had to adhere to the methodology that relies on using some general concepts and the theory, and that is why I also went into command relationships and organisational matters.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. All right. Can we look -- and this is going to be a bit difficulty because it would be preferable if we had had the English up in both versions. You, I think, have got your -- your own copy. But it means that neither of the accused would have it in their own language. But it is easier to see if we see if we look in both the English versions.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So, Your Honours, I'm in the hands of the Defence of this. We can provide, if they haven't already provided their respective clients with hard copy, we probably can get hard copy of the B/C/S report. But, otherwise, it means we're going to have the B/C/S and the English up and then the B/C/S and the English up in the earlier report and it's more difficult to identify. So I'm in the hands of Mr. Krgovic, in particular, as to whether he is happy with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, as far as the Defence is concerned, we have no problem with it. But it -- maybe it would be good if the clients could have both copies at their disposal. Perhaps we should try and procure some as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, one of the suggestions I have is that, helpfully, of Mr. Smith is that we can have the two English versions up on e-court and on Sanction, the B/C/S version will come up, we hope.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So can we start, please, General, could you turn -- oh, sorry. May as well let the General -- you've got your report with you, I believe, General?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Sorry, Ms. Korner, we are advised that that suggestion wouldn't work because on Sanction the Court Officer then loses control.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, let's -- first of all, please, can we start then and we'll see how it goes. Let's have the B/C/S and the English. The English report is 0031 -- sorry, the present report is 0031D2, and the Popovic report, which is at tab 100 of our bundle, is 20232. So can we start with page five in each report; first of all, the English. Unfortunately, there are no paragraphs, or the paragraphs don't equate in the Popovic report.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, under -- in this -- your present report, paragraph 14 you talk about the armed conflict in Bosnia and Herzegovina. The parties to the conflict were the Army of the Republic of Bosnia, the Croatian Defence Council, and the Army of the RS. "Each with their own paramilitary and parapolice forces." Do you see that in paragraph 14.

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, can we have up, please, the same page in the Popovic report, page 5.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Five, in the Popovic report. Not six. Oh, yes, is that -- no, that's -- 5 is right in English, but I don't think it's the same page in B/C/S. Got page 6 up there. Page 5 in B/C/S as well. I'll say it again: Page 5. No -- oh, I see. All right. I see, okay. One page back apparently in e-court. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Do you see there, it's paragraph 2, which is almost identical, just slight change of wording, and it may be translation, but you say there: [As read] "The Army of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Croatian Defence Council on one side, the Army of Republika Srpska on the other were at war. Paramilitary forces took part on both sides." You don't mention or you didn't mention in the Popovic report parapolice. Why was that? Why did you introduce the word "parapolice" into this report?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, both reports were authored by me. And you will allow for the right of the author to change some parts or re-use them as a whole if I wrote them.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. I -- I quite understand. Of course, you have the right to do that. I'm simply asking why you introduced the word "parapolice" when you wrote this report?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose it's because the second report has more to do with the police, as we all know. And that was probably the reason why I introduced the term.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. But you're giving a general, as it were, overview in both reports, and you're saying, These are the combatants on either side of the divide, as it were, and they don't change, do they, simply because the police is about the police in this case, but not about the police in General Gvero?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Korner. But in the trial, because of which I'm here now, the focus is on 1992, in which year, as we have seen, only about halfway through the year, the defence system in the Army of Republika Srpska was -- was made legal.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, General. What you were talking about in both paragraphs in both reports was the forces in 1992 when the conflict broke out. So why did you mention parapolice in this report and not in the last report?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, for one thing, these are three questions, merged into one. And, secondly, if Ms. Korner wants to quote the paragraph, she should also point out that in the Gvero report, the period is from 1992 through 1995; whereas, this here deals only with 1992. So it is not the same period referred to.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I agree. It's -- but it starts in 1992. But this is a small point and I'm going to ask just one other question.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: General, what on -- sorry. What do you mean by "parapolice"? You see, you were asked that at page 23647, and you explained -- well, you didn't explain, I suggest -- I'm sorry, 23645, and all you said was: [As read] "All these newly formed forces" - and this is 23646 - "were accompanied by a number of different paramilitary and parapolice forces?" So please tell us what do you call a parapolice force as opposed to a paramilitary force?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, from the start of the armed conflict, armed conflicts in the former Yugoslavia, from Slovenia, through Croatia, to Bosnia-Herzegovina, I had personal experience with parapolice forces because I met them. When the conflicts broke out, the practice in those republics was that there were regular police forces of the Ministry of the Interior, but, in parallel, some individuals put on uniforms, set up check-points of their own accord, and stopped JNA members. For example, in Croatia, there was the regular MUP and besides, there were parapolice forces that we colloquially called Zengas and they were not controlled by the MUP, or at least as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But, are you simply saying that armed men wearing uniform, and by that I take it you mean camouflage, who were setting up check-points you're calling parapolice?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think this is not a correct interpretation of what this witness said, because if Ms. Korner wants to quote the witness she has to quote everything that he said, not to pick out one characteristic of the forces that the witness is talking about.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. I am picking out what he has just said: "Some individuals put on uniforms, set up check-points of their own accord and stopped JNA members."

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And they're out of control and command of regular MUP.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Don't -- don't give evidence, Mr. Krgovic. But I don't know to what extent, as Ms. Korner has indicated, we're dealing with a translation problem, but I, too, am curious about what the witness means, and I would invite her to head down the path she is headed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right, General, are you calling parapolice armed men in camouflage uniform who set up check-points and stopped the JNA?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, once the armed conflicts broke out --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continued] ...

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- and all the way to --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I'm going to stop you. Because unless you answer my questions directly we will be here for a lot, lot longer. Now, please, answer the question directly: Are you calling parapolice forces men in camouflage uniform, armed men, who set up check-points and stopped the JNA?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Yugoslav People's Army was the only regular force. That's what I wanted to say. Anyone else was not under its control or under the control of the Territorial Defence units was paramilitary. If it was not under the control of the Ministry of Interior, then we're talking about parapolice forces. And as for specific check-points, I would need to know which check-point is -- that we're talking about, who set it up, whether there was anyone commanding it, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's the whole point, isn't it, General? These were armed men, under allegedly nobody's control, and the generic term, as you used in the Popovic case, is "paramilitary," isn't it?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And I'm asking you, to go back to my original point and let me put it to you directly: Did you end the word "parapolice" in order to assist the Defence of Mr. Zupljanin and for no other reason?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Let me turn to the next part of your report where there are differences.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we go, please, to paragraph 43 in the Popovic -- sorry, in the present report, which is -- I think it's the same page, page 16 in English. And in B/C/S, it should be page 6 still. So that would be -- it's backwards, it's page 5. First of all, let's have a look at the present report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Before we move onto something else, I apologise for not having picked up the points that you tried to elicit from the General. But, General, forgive me, I still quite have not understood why you would call these men parapolice rather than paramilitary or something else. They -- the reason I'm asking is that, on the face of it, these men to whom you referred in your earlier report, would seem to belong to the groups that we have referred to throughout this trial as paramilitary forces. So is there any particular reason why you would link them up with the police by calling them "parapolice forces"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, there were some instances, and I told you that I have come across them, in which policemen would leave their public security stations with their official IDs and use the authority to stop people, maltreat them, but did not take part in specific military operations. They were discharging police duties, but they were not under the control of the regular Ministry of Interior.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Were they dressed in police uniforms?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There were various uniforms. Everyone fetched for himself. They would wear what they could find at home or what they had with them at the moment when they left their stations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I see. Thank you. Please proceed, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] I'm sorry, you say: There were some instances, you came across them, [As read] "in which policemen would leave their public security station with their official IDs and use the authority to stop people, maltreat them, but did not take part in specific military operations." How did come across them?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: While leaving the commands for the units, I sometimes came across those barricades and check-points in the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, I'm sorry. How do you know that the people at the check-points had left their public security stations with their IDs, as opposed to getting false IDs?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm familiar with that fact.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, I think we've dealt with that. If this was something you knew of your own experience, and you've explained that part of your report is from your own experience, why did you not put it into the Popovic report?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, the report which I wrote for the Stanisic and Zupljanin case included mention of these forces because here, in this case, we are dealing with the use of police units in combat operations. Therefore, I wanted to acquaint this Tribunal with the fact that there were also parapolice forces present at the time. Though this is something that is well known.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Are you able to name any of these so-called parapolice forces? In other words, like the Wolves of Vucak, or anything like that?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree with you that it is very difficult, and it was very difficult in practice, to distinguish between paramilitary and parapolice forces. Only in instances when they participated in some combat operations, I would call them paramilitaries. If they stopped people and showed their official IDs, then they acted as parapolice. I know from documents which I have come across that, on the ground, there were, if I remember well, more than 50 paramilitary and such parapolice formations during the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Are you able to tell us what documents?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know the exact number of the document. But I think that this is an report, perhaps from the Main Staff or from the corps command, concerning the existence of these formations, with their names, and the acts they committed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continued] ... Yes.

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mentioned one of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continued] ... Yes, you're talking, I take it, about General Tolimir -- Colonel Tolimir, as he then was, report on paramilitary formations; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think it was that report.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Which you were shown by either Mr. Krgovic, or Mr. Cvijetic - and I can't remember which - when you came here.

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think so. Or perhaps I found that in the footnotes of Mr. Brown's report.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. But you hadn't read it -- well, firstly, were you aware of the existence of Colonel Tolimir's report before you wrote this present report?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: How?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, before we continue with this list, there's still something that is not really clear to me. General, you -- you -- you said in answering a question, Ms. Korner's question: "... policemen would leave their public security station with their official IDs and use the authority to stop people, maltreat them, but did not take part in specific military operations." Then you continue: "They were discharging police duties, but they were not under the control of the regular Ministry of Interior." And then - and I have to find that part - you add: [As read] "On the distinction between paramilitary and parapolice, I would call them paramilitary if they stopped -- I would call them paramilitary," no, sorry. "If they stopped people and showed their official IDs then they acted as parapolice." Do I take it that you mean regular police officers leaving their -- their -- their police building with their IDs, discharging police duties but not under the control of the Ministry of Interior when then they stop people showing their official document, they were parapolice? Is that what you mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely so. And I emphasised, whoever was not under the control of the regular, that is to say, the state-controlled forces. They were then either paramilitaries or the parapolice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: And what makes you conclude that a regular police officer that goes into the street and stops people is not under the control of the Ministry of Interior?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I emphasised: If they were not. That is to say, if they were doing that without permission or without the authorisation of the authorised superior.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: So, in your opinion, that turns them into parapolice?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, it's easier actually if we can do it this way. We've got hard copies for both accused of the B/C/S version of the report. And if we -- those could be handed -- or, the two reports, rather, the one from this case and the one from Popovic. It makes it easier then, if we can have the English up on the screen without the B/C/S. I'll give the B/C/S references. And also for the witness, if he needs it. But I think he has got copies of both his reports. So could we have up on the screen, please, only in English, page 16 of the English report, paragraph, starting: "Formation organisation and tasks ..." And in the Popovic report it will be page 5 in e-court. I want the Popovic -- I don't want two English versions of this report. I want the Popovic report, please. Thank you. No, it's the next -- it's the next page, please. It's page 6.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, very small point, and I don't want to labour it --

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Sorry, sorry --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And in B/C/S could you go to your own reports, please, at paragraph 43 of this report, and it's page ... page 6 of your Popovic report. Now it's a small point, on paragraph 43 of this report, you said: "The war in the former Yugoslav Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina was the result of" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, the witness was trying to signal something.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, I think he was signalling all he has got on the screen is English. But I've given him -- he has his own reports in his own language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I thought.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] ... paragraph in B/C/S which you're reading in the English. So can we have one, maybe, copy for the witness in B/C/S because I think one more is left. Ah, sorry. Please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Well, Your Honours, I was going to try to save time but, in fact, it's just lengthening matters. Could we have, please, page 16, paragraph 43, in English of the present report. And I don't know -- and in B/C/S, the same paragraph. Same page. It's paragraph -- it's the same -- I want the same paragraph in B/C/S, 43. Right. Yes. No. It should be 3. Paragraph 43 in B/C/S. And paragraph 43 in English. In the report in this case, please. Which is 31D2.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. In paragraph 43 in this report you talk about the war was the result of a lack of either will or ability of political leaderships. In paragraph 45, you say: [As read] "It was obvious that the Muslim-Croatian part of the Bosnia-Herzegovina leadership wanted to declare independence of Bosnia and Herzegovina without the agreements [sic] of the representatives of the Serbian people."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And can we go, please, to the next page in each to look at paragraph 49.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You say: {As read] "Territorial Defence units and/or staffs in the municipalities" blah, blah, "paramilitary formations were incorporated into all regular armed formations with different degrees of resubordination." And let's emphasise the word "resubordination" there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now can we go, please, to the same part of your report in Popovic. It is page 6 in English. Sorry, that was a -- Page what? No. Sorry. Yes, page 6 in B/C/S. Sorry, it does. No, sorry. It's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, not -- notwithstanding the break we had this morning, in order to keep to the regular times of sittings, perhaps we could take the break now and these problems can be sorted out when we come back and you continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. That's the difficulty with having English and B/C/S. But, anyhow, I'll try and get the pages more accurately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So we resume in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We now have, General, the equivalent part of your Popovic report with the one we were looking at earlier, which is the formation, manning and organisation of the Army of Republika Srpska. Now, the first unnumbered paragraph here is the equivalent of your paragraph 43, as we looked at earlier, in 43, you talked about a lack of either will or ability of political leaderships. Here, you say it was a consequence of the unwillingness and inability. It's a small point, but why did you change that?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not remember why I changed it, but I don't think it essentially changes the meaning, and I stand by the position that I stated in my later work.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Well, paragraph 3 on this page is the equivalent of the beginning of your paragraph 45. Here, you simply state that "the political leaders of the Serbian people ... on the basis of a popular will ... withdrew from the collective BiH organs ..." In paragraph 45 that we looked at you said that it was obvious that the Muslim-Croatian part of the Bosnia-Herzegovina leadership wanted to declare independence of Bosnia and Herzegovina without the agreement of the representatives of the Serbian people. What made you change the fairly neutral, if I can put that way, political leaders of the Serbian people, to: [As read] "It was obvious that the Muslim-Croatian part of the BH leadership wanted to declare independence," or it should read, really, "the independence of Bosnia and Herzegovina." Which is a criticism, isn't it, of the so-called Muslim-Croatian leadership?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, I stand by what I wrote in paragraph 45 of my latter report.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You may well stand by it, General. My question is: What made you change a neutral proposition to one that is a critical proposition?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To my mind, this is not essential for the topic of the later report that I drafted for this Tribunal, and I do not remember what guided me.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could that have been one of the discussions you had with Mr. Krgovic that made you change that sentence?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not think I discussed this with Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Then in the -- under the A, the formation of the VRS, the paragraph that begins: [As read] "The referendum on the independence of Bosnia and Herzegovina on the 29th and 1st of March, 1992." The equivalent of that in your present report is paragraph 47. You say that in the Popovic report which we have on the screen: "The Serbian people took no part in the referendum?" In your present report, you add: [As read] "International recognition of Bosnia and Herzegovina as an independent state soon followed, accompanied by the inflamed rhetoric of warmongering, increased frequency of armed clashes, and polarisation in the armed forces ..." What made you add that?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, I told you that I had only used parts of this report. You will admit that it was my right as an author to amend or change some of my earlier formulations.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Of course, it's your right, General. And I wouldn't deny that for one moment. But we're interested in -- or at least the Court may like to know, what lay behind your changes, your methodology. So I'm asking you: Why did you add that in to your present report?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I probably had more information when I wrote the new report than at the time when I wrote the first one.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But you -- I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me remind you that I wrote my first report while I was still an active-duty officer; whereas, I was already retired for two years when I wrote my second report, and that gave me more time to read.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But you give no footnote at all for this assertion. So what is it based on? A book? Documents?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is based on known facts that international recognition soon ensued. And in the previous paragraphs, I mentioned the dates of the referendum.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Again, without footnotes, but I'll come back to that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we look then, please, at the next page in -- I think it's -- just let me check that actually. Can we find the part does it say in B/C/S on: "All these armed formations included paramilitary forces ..." Yes, it does, actually. Same page, but with the next page in English, please. It's the penultimate paragraph on that page. Could we look at the next page in English of this report. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [As read] "All these armed formations included paramilitary formations with different levels of subordination to regular military forces." That is the equivalent of your paragraph 49 in the present report but you state there: [As read] "paramilitary formations were incorporated in all regular armed formations with different degrees of resubordination." Now, can you just check, please, because you've got your present report there, I think, that the translation is correct. You say "resubordination" in paragraph 49; and "subordination" in your original report.

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, in both reports, the word used is "potcinjavanje," subordination.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. That's why I thought I'd check. All right. In that case, that is not a point that I wish to pursue.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we go now, please, to -- in the English -- well, let's stick to that report while we're on that page. Could we go to page 8, please, in English, and in B/C/S, to page 7, I think.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Actually, I should have asked you, the word that you've used in both reports originally which you say means subordination -- does it mean subordination or resubordination?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Subordination.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Subordination. Thank you. All right. In this paragraph there, you say: "In the defence and security system of the Republic, the VRS is defined ..." Now it's been translated as "an armed force." Can I ask you, please, just to just read out that sentence, please. Beginning: "In the defence and security system of the Republic ..."

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [As read] "In the defence and security system of the Republic, the VRS is defined as an armed force, the task of which is to defend the sovereignty, territory, independence and constitutional order of Republika Srpska."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So the word which is in B/C/S "kao," k-a-o, means "a," or "an," does it, rather than "the"? In other words, the difference being "an" means -- suggests there is another force. "The" means it is the only armed force. It has been translated as both in the English, so I want to know which is the right translation.

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, this is about the Army of Republika Srpska being an armed force --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continued] ... sorry, my fault. Go on.

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It can be seen from the footnote that I cited that I couldn't formulate it differently from the language used in the law. And that law was adopted in June 1992. And we spoke about this last week and said that there was only the army that was an armed force. 25

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: In the Serbian language there is no article.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm not sure what that means, "there's no article." [Microphone not activated]. There's no "a".

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. The only thing I want to put to you about that is, in fact, the police was an armed force, wasn't it? The police had arms, weapons?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, if we're talking about the international law of war, it is clearly defined there what is to be considered part of the armed forces. At that time, according to the national legislation, the police, under the law cited here, was not part of the armed forces.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continued] ... no, I'm sorry, you misunderstand. The police is not defined as part of the military, if you like, but it was, in reality, an armed force, was it not?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was armed and it became part of the armed forces at the moment when it becomes part of the complement of a military unit, as I have already explained and when the police are commanded by a military officer [Realtime transcript read in error "an officer"].

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We're going slightly sidetracked. There were, in fact, differences between the two reports, but -- at this page, but I want to move on to a rather bigger difference, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm terribly sorry. 27, 10 I believe the witness said "commanded by a military officer." But you can, perhaps, check it out.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, I accept that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you say, General, that the police were commanded by a military officer?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Can we look -- because we might as well stick to one report because otherwise we're going back and forth all the time. Can we look now, please, at page 9 of the report in B/C/S and English under the section C, marked: Organisation. In the second paragraph there, you say: "The extensive nature of the territory of the Republika Srpska and the great length of the front line ..." Yes, C, organisation. So it's the next page, please, in B/C/S. Thank you. [As read] "The extensive nature of the territory of the Republika Srpska and the great length of the front line, as well as certain political beliefs, led to tactical units being organised on the territorial principle ..." Now can we have a look, please, at the report for this case, at paragraph 65. Yes, if we can perhaps highlight it in the English. There you say: "The extended area of Republika Srpska" instead of "the extensive nature of Republika Srpska," but I think it may be translation: "And the great length of its line of engagement." Before that, it was front line: "As well as certain political beliefs." So that is the same as your Popovic report. But then we get this: [As read] "And the influence of local, particularly municipal, organs of authority on the army and police command and control, led to tactical units being organised on the territorial principle ..." Now those words, "the influence of local, particularly municipal, organs of authority on army and police command and control," have been added by you in this report. Why?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, it is really difficult for me to defend two reports at the same time, even though they're mine. But it's not a problem. This is, again, an extended formulation, and I repeat, that I stand by the language used in the more recent report.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. But I want to know how you came to add that. "The influence of local, particularly municipal ... " Did you add that after you'd had a discussion with Mr. Krgovic? A dilemma?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not remember speaking to Mr. Krgovic about this, but it must certainly be the -- be due to some new insight I gained.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. But is that new insight from Mr. Krgovic who explained to you that part of the defence in this case was to assert that the police were being controlled by the municipal Crisis Staffs. Did he tell you that?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I may have seen that in some documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, there's not a footnote there, nor do you refer to a single Crisis Staff document in your bibliography. So where did you get that from, if not from Mr. Krgovic?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have already told you that I frequently went to the RS. And I mentioned that my brother was a police officer all the time, and still is.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So are you saying that your brother, at some stage between your writing the Popovic report and writing this report, told you that "local, particularly municipal, organs of authority ..." had an influence on the police?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, you are insisting on my refreshing my memory. I'm not sure how I arrived at this very formulation, but I'm sure that it's part of the preparations and the efforts I made when writing my report. And I maintain that it is true.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We go back to the importance of footnoting. But, I'm sorry, I'm going to, as you put it, insist, how is it that you changed in some - you wrote your Popovic report, I think, in 2008 -- almost. March 2008, so exactly three years ago - that you suddenly decided to add that it was "local, particularly municipal, organs of authority" who affected the police, command and control issues in the police and army?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, in the other report, the subject I researched was different. I had to add some elements, in order to emphasise what I was saying so that my expert contribution would be as great as possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. But, you see, you didn't just say about the police. You said it was the army as well. And if it was the army, then why wasn't it in your original Popovic report?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's possible that I left it out in the first report.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Didn't you put it into this report, as I say, because Mr. Krgovic told you that part of the defence in this case was to blame the municipal organs, the Crisis Staffs?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is there anything disputed about the fact in this case that there was some influence of the local organs on the work of the military and the police? I think this is part of the OTP arguments, if they are disputing this.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: This is disgraceful. I am properly cross-examining the General. Interruptions like this to assist the General are improper.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The reason that I'm asking the General this, is not because of what the evidence in the case is but why he changed his report.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, General, I'm asking you for the last time: Did you put that in because of your knowledge of the Defence in this case from Mr. Krgovic, or any other member of his team?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your brother who was a police officer in Prnjavor, what was his rank?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly, but he was one of the people who were in charge at the local police station.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, surely you know what rank. Was he a commander of the police station, chief of the SJB, an inspector?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he was neither of these. But he may have been the head of one of the departments.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, which -- he may have been anything. But which department?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The police department in that particular station. I very rarely talk with him about his specific duties.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But he was able to give you, you tell us, this information about the "influence of local, particularly municipal, organs of authority"?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have told you that because I know. And I told you that I discussed with him because he was fighting in the war for four years. Sometimes he had to leave the local public security station and go as far as 2- or 300 kilometres away.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Would Your Honours forgive me. I just want to check whether I ...

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. While we are on -- this is the last part that I want to ask you about. Paragraph 192 onwards. Page 39 in English. And in B/C/S, it's ... You say in this report: [As read] "The VRS chain of command extends from the president of the republic, in his capacity as the Commander-in-Chief, via the commander of the Main Staff" --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Next page in English, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: "... and commanders down ... to every single individual." Then, 193: [As read] "No persons other than commanders (or, in their absence, chiefs of staff) were ever part of the chain of command ..." 194, you talk about the line of reporting. And then 195: [As read] "All of the above that pertains to the commanding function and the chain of command also pertains to temporary formations and resubordinated units." Again, is the word "subordinated" or "resubordinated"?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The formulation here is "resubordinated units."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. So there it is actually "resubordinated." Now can we look, please, at the equivalent --

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I just add that there is a difference between subordination and resubordination. If you would like me to explain that. Because these notions are not the same.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. And I think you have explained it. A subordinate unit is one that is there and comes under the command during the course of its normal functions, I suppose you can put it; and resubordinated is when you get a unit that would not normally be subordinated that comes under that command. Is that an accurate summary?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, not quite.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. You explain, please. Briefly.

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Resubordination, that we are using here, is a case in which a commander has a certain unit and for the needs of a specific task, he then selects a part of his own unit and attaches it to another unit. So that is the act of resubordinating it. And once this is completed, then the relationship is one of subordination. And there is another case, which is most frequent, when we are talking about police or some other formations which are not part of the unit, then they are attached and this is called attaching them. But, once again, even in such a case the relationship is one of subordination. So we talked about these acts and about the relationship.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Now can we look, please, at your Popovic report at page 15 in English. And I think it's page 14 -- 13 in the B/C/S. Do you see the paragraph that begins: [As read] "The chain of command in the VRS was supposed to extend from the president of the republic as Supreme Commander to the General Staff commander, to the commanders of operational-tactical and tactical units and through all the commanders of smaller units to each individual. However, it was the habit of the president of the republic to command, while disregarding the commander of the General Staff. Contrary to regulations, the Supreme Commander sometimes issued assignments to corps and even brigades." Where do we see any of that in your present report?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not believe that I had to copy everything from the previous report into the new one. In the first part, I referred in the footnote to a formulation that is here.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But, I'm sorry, General. I -- you can change your report, and you have changed your report. In this respect, I'm asking why. Because in your present report, you don't give any of the caveats that we see in this paragraph. So what made you drop the caveats?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. That's all that I want to ask you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, may I ask now, given that we've been through quite a lot of this report, that his Popovic report be made an exhibit in the case, so that the differences are clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I'm not sure I follow why, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Because there are substantial differences between what he's got in the Popovic report on the same topic and those that he has in this report. If, at the end of the day, you decide not to admit his report for this case, then that's fine. But, at the moment, I'm working on the basis that you may decide to admit it; and, therefore, it is important that one can see the differences in the two reports.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic -- sorry, Mr. Zecevic, whichever of you wants to go first.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I do strongly object to this. The position so far in this trial has been that if -- if the issue is on the transcript, which it is, with the -- with the answers -- with the witness's answer on the transcript there is certainly no need to -- to admit another document. I can name a number of instances when -- when -- when that was the -- that was the decision of the Trial Chamber. Especially in a case when we have an expert witness and now we are admitting the expert report which has nothing to do with this. It's from another case. I object to this, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Once again, if this report is to be admitted the problem is with the footnotes because the footnote quoted by Ms. Korner in the specific example talks about the Operation Srebrenica in 1995 and the command, so we would have to admit the footnote with the exhibit which the witness referred to here. Because the question was taken out of the context of the report. And that would bring us into a situation where we would have to include all these parts. Because specifically when Ms. Korner talked about the part that was left out, what is mentioned is a specific transcript and a specific event from 1995. So we should include that transcript as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] ... the point has been lost slightly. This is previous, we suggest, previous inconsistent statements made by this witness. It goes wholly and completely to the credibility of his report in this case and his credibility as a witness. It is therefore important that if anybody wants to check - it's got nothing to do with the admitting of the footnotes - we need to have that report there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, as Mr. Krgovic has said, and I fully appreciate the path you have gone down of challenging the witness's credibility on previous inconsistent statements. But as Mr. Zecevic has said, the relevant parts have been put to him and are now part of the transcript. Why do we need to burden ourselves with this report? For the Trial Chamber itself to conduct a side by side compare and contrast exercise.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If necessary, Your Honours. I have skipped some things. There are other parts of that report that are different. Your Honours, unless it's made an exhibit - and I confess, I fail to see the difficulty with this - there's no way of dealing with it. It's not enough to say -- otherwise I'm going to take up even more time by going through other differences. But, Your Honour, my suggestion, clearly put, is that there are differences. And one of the matters that Your Honours will have to consider is what those differences are and -- and -- and, I suppose, how major they are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: The Chamber is not persuaded that this earlier report should be admitted. The -- it is it patent from the record the challenge that the Prosecution has made to the credibility of the witness based on what, in the Prosecution's view, are inconsistent statements. And no doubt at the appropriate stage arguments would be advanced along those lines. But we see no need to admit this earlier report as a separate exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I want to turn, General, now to the footnotes in your present report. Would you accept that in comparison with the reports you looked at over the weekend from Dr. Nielsen and Mr. Brown, your report is very sparsely footnoted?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And, as we established when I first asking [sic] you questions, would you accept that it is important when coming to conclusions to, first of all, look at the original, or copies of original documents if possible?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And that if footnoting, it's important to be accurate in -- in the -- the quote that you take from the book or from the document?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I want to start, first of all, with the footnote to your paragraph 50. Footnote number 10. And that's page 17 in English of your report. That's paragraph 50. Footnote number 10. You cite, for the decision on the withdrawal, a book by some people called Pavlovic and Popovic. And can we just have a look at that, please. It is 20235, and it's tab 97. Do you agree -- it's a photocopy that we've been provided of this book that you've relied on entitled: "Succession orchestrated by the great powers." Is that right?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we look, then, please, at the -- published in -- the next page showing that it was published in Belgrade in 1996. And then the page thereafter in English which is the third page, and I hope it's -- the introduction. [As read] "The disintegration of the SFRY began with Slovenia's violent secession but the flames of the civil war were fanned by the newly formed Croatian Democratic Party's leadership. With their violent secession, Slovenia and Croatia committed an aggression against the state of the SFRY and, together about Bosnia and Herzegovina's Muslims, started a civil war, causing immense human casualties and suffering in the territory of the former Yugoslavia." If we skip the next sentence: "Not even the apocalyptic [sic] vision of a bloody civil war could deter primeval, hate-fueled secessionists from their plans." Would you agree that this is a very, very, one-sided view of the conflict?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, in my work, I cited in the footnote what exactly it was that I took from this book. I did not use this introduction for my report.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, we'll see that. But why did you use this book?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I had it in my personal library. It was written by people who have the highest qualifications. It was issued by the -- published by the Institute for Political Studies, which is an institution that has a good reputation. And I used it because, in the time that I had at my disposal, I could not find the original order on the withdrawal of units of JNA, which I needed, and I was aware that this piece of information was exactly quoted in this book.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. But we'll come to that right now. But you say you couldn't find it. And you were dependent, to a certain extent, on Mr. Krgovic's provision of documents to you. Did you ever ask Mr. Krgovic, Is there a copy of the JNA withdrawal order that you could let me see?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, I believed that to confirm this fact, it was sufficient to rely on a scientific and publicly published work, which included this information about the order and the withdrawal of JNA units. And I do not see anything that can be contested about this piece of information.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Well, let's have a look at another part of this scientific public work.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could we go, please, in English to page 24.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm not sure where this line of questioning of Ms. Korner is taking us. We are discussing a date, which is not at stake. So what is the purpose of showing the witness another paragraph from the book and saying that the book is like this or like that. The witness said clearly why he used this book as a source of reference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic, I confess I agree with you entirely. Ms. Korner, the -- how -- how is this -- if -- if the passages to which you have referred and I don't know, of course, what you -- what other passages you intend to refer the witness to are not passages that he relied or cited with approval, where does this take us?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, in order to explain that, I'm going to ask the witness to leave court. I'm really sorry that Your Honour cannot see it, and I will explain it, if Your Honours will allow me to explain it, when I finish the part of the examination. But, otherwise I would have to ask the witness to leave court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: How long would it -- the reason why I'm asking is that we're 15 minutes away from the adjournment and I'm wondering if the witness being excused now should not think of returning until 12.25.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, Your Honours, I'd like to finish this, it's very short and then move to the next footnote. And when he has left, I can explain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: You're asking him to leave now.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I misunderstood you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm asking to be allowed to continue this line of cross-examination, with an explanation as to why I'm pursuing this when we -- just before the break.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Otherwise, I will have to ask the witness to leave court because he does speak English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, it appears to us that this is, for the moment, irrelevant. So we would ask the witness to be excused so that you can make your case as to why you should be permitted to continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the reason that I'm asking these questions and putting another part of the book to him which is actually opposite where he obtained this quote from, is to show that the witness is, to put it simply, an unapologetic Serb nationalist and apologist who is using books as part of his reading, if you like, for the preparation of these paper [sic] which are not proper academic books at all. Your Honour, you will see that most of the assertions he makes are totally unfootnoted. And, therefore, it is important, which would submit, for the Court to see what he is relying on for his version of events, which is not documents at all, because he hasn't seen any, but books like this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: But, Ms. Korner, isn't it a common experience that no matter what field we're talking about in history, politics, religion, that there would be authors whose views may generally be held to be quite odious but somewhere buried in the pile of whatever, there is a germ of truth, and isn't a witness entitled to mine for material in wherever it's likely to be found. I appreciate, from the passages that you have seen, that this is -- this -- this book may be dismissed as a polemic, anti- -- pro-Serb tirade but it does necessarily follow from those criticisms which attach to the book that the portions on which the -- the witness relied undermines his credibility. The logic of that, with respect, I can't follow.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But, Your Honours, you will see that on a number of occasions during the actual report, particularly the beginning parts, he gives a view of the conflict clearly not based, because he has not seen any of the documents, the beginnings and particularly the VRS, which he has already said are based on his background reading and, Your Honour, this and he say this is one of the books in his library. It is not surprising, we would submit that -- that the sort of views he expresses in his report in his general sections are written in the way that they are. And unless Your Honours see what he is relying on, you cannot assess that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: But the point that you made about -- you -- you made it today, I think you made it one day last week, in terms of his methodology that his - the paucity on the primary sources on which he relies, seriously affects the worth of the finished product, and, ultimately, therefore, the weight, for our purposes the Trial Chamber would give to it. Isn't that sufficient without going down this road?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, I'm hoping to persuade Your Honours that it goes a great deal further than giving it weight, that at the end of the day it should be, under Rule 95, struck out because there has to come a point where the Trial Chamber should say, This can't go on. But that's to jump ahead. Your Honours, if Your Honours feel that his evident bias is already present then I won't pursue this. Because as I say, this comes out because he takes the 4th of May decision from -- not only from the main part of this -- this -- this tome but from a footnote which doesn't give the document either. So Your Honours, if that's evident, Your Honours, then I won't pursue it but I can't take anything for granted. And it is really important, in our submission, that Your Honours have the full picture how this man came to write the report and his background knowledge, the source of his background knowledge, his experience, which he is relying on. So that's the submissions that I make on why I'm doing this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I understood the -- the leave of the Trial Chamber to Ms. Korner is to -- to explain to us why she wants to insist on this particular answer and showing this particular book. However, what Ms. Korner is doing is she is testifying and making the submissions on the expert report, which I don't think it is appropriate at this point. Now, Your Honours, I do object, because it is, a simply and very clearly, and the witness -- the expert answered two times: I used this book for particular reason. The date of the order to withdraw. That is the only thing. So the footnote confirms the date of the order of the withdrawal of the -- of the army from Bosnia and Herzegovina. There is nothing from that book that he took except the date of the order. And he wrote that in his -- in his -- in -- in his expert report, and explained over here. So I don't see any basis for Ms. Korner to claim what she claimed and made -- made a submission as she did, and to answer any other question on this particular book. Because this book was used for the purposes for the very specific purpose of the date of the order, which the witness knows by the -- by the way the -- that is his testimony, that he knows that the order exists. He just -- and he knows that the -- that the date is accurate. I don't really see where we are with going in this respect. I -- I must say, that I think that with all due respect that Ms. Korner is just using up the time because we are not going to the merit of -- of the witness's -- witness's expert report for the fourth day in a row. We're discussing -- I know that Ms. Korner is entitled to test the credibility of the witness, and I don't have a problem with that. I surely -- I hope that the Trial Chamber will understand that as I understand it. That -- but I don't want to make submissions at this point. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zecevic. Do you wish to add anything, Mr. Krgovic [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I fully agree with what Mr. Zecevic said.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: First, Your Honour, this is it not Mr. Zecevic's witness, and Mr. Zecevic has a vested interest, as well as Mr. Krgovic, from preventing this. But it really is important because it is not just the contents of the report. But when you get something like this, using material like this, for whatever reason, and the suggestion that we make, and I think he has already confirmed it, is that he thinks -- I think he said it was a scientific -- it was written by persons of the highest qualifications and it is scientific and all the rest of it. Now, Your Honours, it is important --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, I haven't had the time to check all the footnotes, but are you able to tell us whether the General, in his report, refers to this book in other footnotes than footnote 10?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think so. So I would have to double-check that. But I think he does. Because I just picked on this particular footnote.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think not, Your Honour. I believe that this is the only citation.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continued] ... Mr. Smith has just checked and that's the only citation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Well, we're near the break, so we will resume at 12.25.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Before the witness is escorted back to the stand, the Chamber has one question of Ms. Korner to which it requires a short answer. And that is whether you're in a position to, if you are permitted to continue along this line of cross-examination of the witness, point to any portion of his report which you could then argue or suggest has its origin in this book that you're presently -- that you presently have up.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Do you mean a direct quote from the book?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Not necessarily a direct quote. But we thought we understood your line of questions to be that -- apart from the specific citation in the footnote that we all agree is what the witness admitted he relied on this book for. We thought that the purpose of your intended line of questions was that the witness's -- that -- that you would be in a position, if permitted to continue, to show that the witness -- that this witness's report --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, if you go to -- there's no direct quote. What I'm putting to the witness is that his line of thinking, particularly in regard to the part of his report headed: Formation, organisation and tasks of the armed forces of Republika Srpska, is heavily influenced by his reading of matter such as the book that I have just pointed to. We better have the screen, please, the section, Formation organisation and tasks of the armed forces of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: We don't know that we need the details.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Oh, I see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Your answer is you think can.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I would suggest that certainly part of that is based not just on the book, but his general reading of books which, as I put it, are one-sided, as background to what he wrote in his report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So when the witness comes back in, we would permit you to continue. And you're on a short leash, Ms. Korner. And we expect that the -- the rest of time you have allotted to you, you would move into the substance of his report.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. I realise -- I've done very little so far, strangely enough. It was only about three and a half hours by the end of Friday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] It's now five hours and ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, so could the witness be conducted back to the stand, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: General, just before we go to the actual part where you took the quote from, I was showing you a part of the book - I don't know what we've got up at the moment - it should be page 24 in English. Yes, it is. And the same in -- Do you see the paragraph in the B/C/S that begins: "Instead of having a calming effect ..." which is on the previous page in English. Is it up on the page. I can't tell. Is there a paragraph there that begins: "Instead of having a calming effect ..."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, there isn't in the English, Your Honours. The part of the English that I want to refer to is that first paragraph which actually begins -- I'm almost beginning to think that isn't worth the effort, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: General, just answer the question, would you kind enough, is there a paragraph in front of you on the page in B/C/S, that begins: "Instead of having a calming effect ..." Is that the first paragraph?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Towards the end of that first paragraph, do we see these words: [As rea] "All barracks in towns where the Muslims and Croats were the majority population were exposed to fierce and unprovoked attacks. The Serb civilian population was exposed to the same acts. By means of horrific crimes over helpless elderly people, women, and even children, the Serb population was also threatened with physical extermination. By that time, it had already become clear that the Muslim-Croatian leadership had opted for the use of force against the Serb people and the JNA in Bosnia and Herzegovina." Now, General, as we'll see when we come to it, you adopted part of that paragraph, didn't you in your own report?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the Prosecutor please specify in which part of his report.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Paragraph 46. No, let's not go there. I don't want to change documents. It takes too long. Thank you. We'll come to it. I assure you we'll come it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you that was an accurate description of what happened, General?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, I have already said in which part I used this book. I used it only to quote the date of the decision on the withdrawal of the JNA from Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, we'll come to this in a moment, or I suggest at least part of that report, part of your report at paragraph 46 contains part of this paragraph in slightly different words, I agree. But I'm asking you now whether you believe that this description of what happened, namely, that barracks in towns where Muslims and Croats were the majority population were exposed to fierce and unprovoked attacks. The Serb civilian option was exposed to the same acts? Do you believe that that is an accurate description of what happened?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, I stand by the positions I put forward in my report. If you are actually -- if that's what you're getting at.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, I'm asking you, please, General, whether, based on this book which you think is academic and whatever - I don't remember your exact words now - you accept that this description of what happened is an accurate account of the events --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one question: Are you now examining the witness as an expert, or are you trying to elicit information he got personally?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: For the nth time, I would ask the Court --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Please continue, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. General, do you accept from your reading of this book and which you used for the basis of definitely the cite about the 4th of May, is an accurate account of what happened?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot confirm that because this was written by other people. These are not my words. I include an account of these events in my report and I stand by it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Let's go to paragraph 46 and the quote that you use -- sorry, the, quote that you used it for, can we go to 52, please -- sorry, in the book. Can we go to the next page in the book. Sorry, it's page 109, page 52 of the translation. Yep. There we see: [As read] "the SFRY Presidency decision of the 4th of May for all JNA members ... to pull out -- to pull out of the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina. And no later than May 19th ... did not contribute to the conflicts stopping, nor did it ease them. On the contrary, in the period of these JNA members pulling out, they were exposed to treacherous and perfidious attacks in which serious losses were inflicted on them." And if we look at the footnote for that, it's all about manipulation of the Muslim-Croat part of the Bosnia-Herzegovina leadership concerning the extraction of cadets from the military high school from Sarajevo. And that's, again, unquoted. So we don't know where he got that from, or the author has got that from. All right. Can we now go, please, to paragraph 46 of your present report. You say: "The role of the Yugoslav People's Army was to prevent interethnic armed conflict." I'll come back to that one later. [As read] "Hostility towards the JNA gradually developed in Bosnia and Herzegovina just as it had done in Slovenia and Croatia. The army, its members, and facilities were subject to provocations and attacks. The aim was to provoke the army into a combat engagement that would justify secession. The Muslim and Croatian political leadership in Bosnia-Herzegovina conducted a propaganda campaign branding the JNA an aggressor and the Serbian Chetnik army ...," and so on and do forth. There is no footnote for these assertion. Where did you get that from?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, we received much information from our superior commands. And, based on that, I briefed our personnel.
